title: Teachers' Use of Time and Student Achievement https://www.nber.org/system/files/working_papers/w30686/w30686.pdf
author: Barton, Craig
source: Tips for Teachers (tipsforteachers.co.uk), November 14, 2024 — original paper:
summary: This entry summarizes a National Bureau of Economic Research working paper by Burgess, Taylor and Rawal on how English secondary teachers' choices about class-time allocation relate to GCSE outcomes, as covered by Barton. Using classroom observations and a structured effectiveness rubric, the researchers find that the best use of time differs by subject: maths results improve when more time goes to individual practice and assessment, while English results improve when more time is spent on students working and talking with classmates. Crucially, these time-allocation effects hold even after controlling for a teacher's rated instructional effectiveness, implying that changing what a teacher spends time on can raise achievement independent of the teacher's underlying skill level. The paper also validates that lightly trained peer observers can generate useful feedback on these patterns, and it reconfirms the established link between rubric-rated teacher effectiveness and student achievement.
points: The optimal use of class time is subject-specific: more individual practice and assessment helps in maths, while more peer talk and collaborative work helps in English.

Time-allocation effects on achievement hold even after controlling for a teacher's rated instructional skill — meaning changing what time is spent on can raise outcomes without any change in teacher ability.

A concrete estimate: maths students in classes where teachers allocate 'most' rather than 'some' time to practice and assessment score around 0.08 standard deviations higher, teacher skill held constant.
Peer teachers with only minimal training were able to give useful, actionable feedback through classroom observation, supporting peer observation as a practical improvement lever.
quotes: This research paper from the National Bureau of Economic Research examines how teachers' choices about how to allocate class time influence student performance on GCSE exams in England.

The researchers find that teachers make different choices regarding time allocation and these choices are associated with student achievement. In math, students perform better when their teacher spends more time on individual practice and assessment, while in English, more time spent working and talking with classmates leads to better outcomes.

Notably, these relationships hold even when controlling for teacher instructional effectiveness, suggesting that changes to classroom instruction can improve student learning even without improvements in teacher skills.

For example, students in a math class where the teacher allocates “most of the time” to practice and assessment would be expected to score about 0.08σ higher than students in a class where the teacher only allocates “some of the time” to practice and assessment, even if the teacher's skill level remains the same.

Peer observation can be an effective method for gaining insight into the differences in teaching. The study found that peer teachers with minimal training were able to provide effective feedback to their colleagues.
These results suggest opportunities to improve student achievement without changes in teachers' skills.
